title: Hudson Williams Debuts ‘Scary Hot’ Blue Eyes in First ‘Yaga’ Clip at San Diego Comic-Con
description:
Fans got a sneak peek at Hudson Williams’ starring role in “Yaga” on Saturday afternoon.

	A clip from Crave’s upcoming mystery thriller was shown d
body:
Fans got a sneak peek at Hudson Williams’ starring role in “Yaga” on Saturday afternoon.

	A clip from Crave’s upcoming mystery thriller was shown during a panel at San Diego Comic-Con, featuring series cast members Noah Reid (“Schitt’s Creek”), Clark Backo (“Venom: The Last Dance”), Letterkenny), Carrie-Anne Moss (“Memento”) and showrunner and executive producer Kat Sandler. 

	Recording wasn’t allowed for the exclusive SDCC clip but, according to those in attendance, it began with a shot of a witch before jumping to Reid and Williams’ characters meeting for the first time. It also debuted Williams’ blue eyes, which were first revealed in first-look photos earlier this week.
	

	While Williams wasn’t in attendance, he recorded a video message for the packed room. “I wish I could be there with you today, and that beautiful cast and crew that I love so much,” he said. “I’ve also never been to Comic-Con so I’d really love to be there!”


	“The show was a blast,” he continued. “It was a wild one to film and I just hope you guys love it as much as I had fun filming it.”

	“Yaga,  based on Sandler’s hit play, reimagines the myth of Baba Yaga and centers on Radd (Reid), a private investigator who arrives in a small coastal town to investigate the disappearance of a young heir to a powerful fishery, Henry Park (Williams). He finds himself at odds with an apprehensive local detective, Carson (Clark Backo), a charismatic university professor with a taste for younger men, Katherine (Carrie-Anne Moss) and a labyrinth of enigmatic suspects.

	“I am the smartest showrunner in the world,” Sandler said about snagging Williams for the show after his breakout success in “Heated Rivalry.” “We’re very lucky that he wanted to come play.”
	

	“You’ll get to see another side of Hudson’s acting capabilities,” Reid added. “It’s a wild performance. He’s got blue eyes, which everyone’s been commenting on. It’s like ‘Oh that’s kind of scary hot.’”

schema.headline: Hudson Williams Debuts ‘Scary Hot’ Blue Eyes in First ‘Yaga’ Clip at San Diego Comic-Con

title: ‘Love Island USA’ Contestant Kenzie Slams Rumors That She’s a Trump Supporter ‘Just Because I’m Blonde and White’: ‘F— the F— Off!’
description:
“Love Island USA” Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis has slammed rumors that she is a Trump supporter.

	Speculation started spreading amongst the “Lo
body:
“Love Island USA” Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis has slammed rumors that she is a Trump supporter.

	Speculation started spreading amongst the “Love Island” fandom early in the season after fans started posting unverified screenshots from Kenzie’s Instagram account of her standing in front of Trump flags. On Thursday, she directly addressed the claims while on an Instagram livestream.


	“That’s so funny ‘cause I’m not a Trump supporter, so you guys can fuck the fuck off!” she said. “Just because I’m blonde and white doesn’t mean I’m a fucking Trump supporter. What the hell?”
	

	Kenzie was a contestant on the most recent season of “Love Island USA,” the ultra-popular dating show where a group of ready-to-mingle singles are dropped into Fiji to see if they can find true love. The audience is able to vote on who gets dumped from the island based on which couples are most compatible, including choosing the winning couple that ultimately gets awarded $100,000.

	While on the show, Kenzie had the most connections out of everyone, starting out the season with Zach Georgiou before being recoupled with Corbin Mims. She eventually got paired up with Caleb McDaniel and, after Casa Amor, met Dylan Wrona. The two were voted out of the villa right before finale night.

	Kenzie left the season before finale night with her final connection, Dylan, and the two recently made their relationship official. On Friday, Dylan wrote in an Instagram post: “Getting to know you in the villa was unforgettable, but falling for you in the real world was all too easy. It didn’t take me long to realize there was no other way — I had to make you my girlfriend! And what better place to do it than on the top of NYC.”
	

	As the “Love Island USA” contestants get adjusted back to reality, fans can look forward to the official reunion episode, which will air Monday, Aug. 31 on Peacock at 6 p.m. PT/9 p.m. ET.

schema.headline: ‘Love Island USA’ Contestant Kenzie Slams Rumors That She’s a Trump Supporter ‘Just Because I’m Blonde and White’: ‘F— the F— Off!’

title: ‘EverQuest Legends’ Unveils Cat Race Kerran as Playable Characters for Video Game Franchise’s Reboot (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The upcoming “EverQuest” reboot video game, “EverQuest Legends,” will launch with the 25-year-old franchise’s fan-favorite Kerran cat race as playab
body:
The upcoming “EverQuest” reboot video game, “EverQuest Legends,” will launch with the 25-year-old franchise’s fan-favorite Kerran cat race as playable characters.

	The announcement was made Saturday at San Diego Comic-Con’s “EverQuest Legends” panel, just days ahead of the game’s July 28 launch.

	“In our game, we’re excited to announce for the first time that we will have a playable race called Kerran,” “EverQuest Legends” executive producer David “Sysyphus” Youssefi told Variety in an interview ahead of Comic-Con. “They will be the same type of creatures you see on Kerra Isle in the original game, so not the version that was translocated to the moon. And much like the Frogloks, we’re excited that we’re going to be reimagining this player race in the original art style of the game. We’re taking those original models and updating the skins and updating the animations to make them actually a playable character race, and that will be available at launch.”
	

	Variety has the exclusive first-look images of the Kerran race of playable characters in “EverQuest Legends,” which can be viewed at the bottom of this post.


	Developed by first-time studio Game Jawn in collaboration with publisher Daybreak, “EverQuest Legends” is a reimagining of the original 1999 MMO game made by community members who are all self-professed mega fans of the franchise.

	While kept under wraps until now, having the Kerran as a playable character option in the reboot has been a key component for the dev team, despite the fact Kerran weren’t a playable race in the original “EverQuest,” but were in “EverQuest II.”
	

	“First of all, everyone loves cats,” Youssefi says of the decision to include the Kerran. “The Kerran race is a cat race. It’s sort of a tribal race from an area in the game called Kerra Isle. One of the key features of ‘EverQuest Legends’ is the fact that we’re not really tied directly to the history or the lore of the other ‘EverQuest’ games, so we’re kind of taking our own direction.”

	Youssefi adds: “And in ‘EverQuest I,’ there was a Kerran race on Kerra Isle, but it was not a playable character. It wasn’t until a later expansion, when according to the lore of the game, some of the Kerran creatures were translocated to the moon of Luclin. They became a different type of cat race called the Vah Shir. So in ‘EverQuest I,’ the cat race that you can actually play as a player is called the Vah Shir, and it looks different, and it’s a different timeline of the game.”

	The choice was made due to both internal and external demand, per Youssefi.

	“I think that we knew pretty early on in the project that this is something that we wanted,” the “EverQuest Legends” executive producer says. “Just to give you an example, on Kerra Isle, in our version of the game, we’ve renamed all the NPCs after the development team’s real-life cats.”

	Youssefi adds: “But I will say that over the last few months, the outcry and demand from the player base for the Kerran race has sort of exploded. So it is clearly both internal and the fan base. We all want the Kerran.”

	“EverQuest Legends” aims to capture the essence of the original game while also incorporating is also new features and quality of life improvements. In particular, “EverQuest Legends” has been designed to appeal to solo and casual gamers, while still including groups (of up to 4 players) and raids (up to 8 players).

	“I think what we want people to know is ‘EverQuest Legends’ is really unique in that we’ve gone back to the original game of ‘EverQuest’ from 1999 and reimagined that,” Youssefi says. “It’s somewhat of a preservation project, in that we’ve had to go back and recreate some of the original zones, and then create new characters in the old art style, like the Frogloks and Kerran. And a lot of care and attention went into recreating the game that we remember from 1999, those of us who are old enough to have actually played it back then, and it’s a really special and magical game that had a lot of immersiveness to it.”
	

	Youssefi says he thinks the “EverQuest Legends” team has both “recaptured that and we’ve modernized the game so that it is more approachable for a casual player or has more modern game features than the original game did.”

	“But it’s also an opportunity for people who played the game back then to enjoy it again, but in a more casual and relaxed way,” Youssefi says.

schema.headline: ‘EverQuest Legends’ Unveils Cat Race Kerran as Playable Characters for Video Game Franchise’s Reboot (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Futurama’ to Release Three New Supersized Specials, Including a Christmas Episode, Starting Next Year on Hulu
description: Hulu has greenlit three supersized “Futurama” specials in addition to the show’s upcoming Season 14, the series’ executive producers and cast reveal
body:
Hulu has greenlit three supersized “Futurama” specials in addition to the show’s upcoming Season 14, the series’ executive producers and cast revealed Saturday at San Diego Comic-Con.

	During their morning Comic-Con panel, which featured creator Matt Groening, showrunner and head writer David X. Cohen and more cast and crew, the “Futurama” team unveiled a trailer for Season 14, which returns on Monday, Aug. 3. They also shared details about the three extended length “Futurama” specials (dubbed “XXXL-Sized”), which are currently in production and will kick off in 2027 with an Xmas-related edition.
	

	Here’s the logline for Season 14: “Brace yourselves… The future is about to get a whole lot stranger! It’s a non-stop onslaught of swaggering space pirates, lab-grown meats, sexy scams… plus the shocking return of Dr. Zoidberg’s lost love! You didn’t see that coming, prior to being told about it just now! It’s a thrilling, all-new season of ‘Futurama’ on Hulu!”


	Season 14 of “Futurama” premieres Monday, August 3 with two new episodes on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+ (for bundle subscribers) and Disney+ internationally, with new episodes streaming every Monday. Here’s the trailer:



	John DiMaggio, Billy West, Katey Sagal, Tress MacNeille, Maurice LaMarche, Lauren Tom, Phil Lamarr and David Herman star in “Futurama.” The series was created by Matt Groening and developed by Groening and David X. Cohen. Executive Producers include Groening, Cohen, Ken Keeler and Claudia Katz.

	20th Television Animation, a part of Disney Television Studios, is the studio on “Futurama,” with animation by Rough Draft Studios.

schema.headline: ‘Futurama’ to Release Three New Supersized Specials, Including a Christmas Episode, Starting Next Year on Hulu

title: ‘Brunello: The Gracious Visionary’ Review: Giuseppe Tornatore’s Seductive Hagiography of a Fashion Legend
description: As a design house, Brunello Cucinelli is a name synonymous with luxury and quality. As a production company, it’s hard to know how to feel about it
body:
As a design house, Brunello Cucinelli is a name synonymous with luxury and quality. As a production company, it’s hard to know how to feel about it preceding a biographical film about its namesake. “Brunello: The Gracious Visionary” tells the story of the fashion luminary from his humble beginnings in rural Perugia, Italy to the heights of his success as an international tastemaker and proponent of what he calls “humanistic capitalism.”
	

	Described by veteran Italian director Giuseppe Tornatore (“Cinema Paradiso”) as “neither a documentary, nor a feature film, nor a commercial,” it qualifies best as hagiography. But with as skilled a filmmaker at the helm as Cucinelli is a designer and entrepreneur, one may not mind being swept along by its rhapsodic portrait, even if you quickly become convinced that “The Gracious Visionary” is too generous to be fully honest about its subject.


	Born in 1956, Cucinelli grew up on a farm where he learned important lessons from rustic living; daily meals around the family table cultivated an appreciation for the wisdom (and company) of his elders, while the responsibilities of making straight furrows while plowing the family fields taught him the value of beauty. Tornatore enlists Cucinelli to narrate his childhood, then recreates it in vivid detail so the designer can literally walk back through his own memories. It’s the sort of nostalgia at which the filmmaker excels, and you can practically feel the earthy heat, emanating from the downstairs cowshed, that kept the young boy and his relatives warm during the winter.
	

	By the time Tornatore depicts Brunello running carefree through fields of gold and red flowers, dragging a handmade kite behind him, it’s clear he’s aiming for something more beatific than a simple history lesson. Recalling the biblical knights that danced and fought in Cucinelli’s childhood dreams, the director projects crayon drawings on the rafters above the bed his fictional counterpart (Francesco Cannevale) shares with his cousins. In interview segments, the designer’s genteel delivery makes it sound like he’s confiding in you, even though he’s clearly told these stories over and over. (In fact, his wife Federica says exactly that, as do daughters Camilla and Carolina, and any number of employees and colleagues.)

	What’s surprising about Tornatore’s approach is how unhurried he is in getting to the details that people familiar with the brand are likely most interested in. The film takes more than an hour to get to Cucinelli’s first inklings as a business owner, much less conceiving the vivid garments that his admirers argue “invented color cashmere.” (Amusingly, a relative observes that well into his twenties, he lived “a life of leisure.” Cucinelli counters: “I didn’t see it as doing nothing, I saw it as enriching my soul.” Slackers, make sure to put that one in your back pocket next time someone asks about your future.)

	Even then, Tornatore bounces between pivotal inspirations — a hated pair of green corduroy pants given as a teen, a beloved caramel coat that later formed the cornerstone of his menswear line — and the familial interactions that shaped his professional philosophies, such as witnessing his father’s despair after obtaining a manufacturing job that left him feeling dehumanized. Framed by the designer’s skill as a card player (oh yeah, his first way of making money as a teen was as a card sharp), Cucinelli’s scrappy ambition catapulted him to success through a series of calculated risks which everyone from Oprah to spiritual leaders recount in hushed, amazed tones.

	Yet amidst the designer’s humanistic attitudes and slavish devotion to beauty, the questions are never asked why the price point of his clothes is prohibitive to everyone but the most affluent customers, or if the workers he seems to treat so well are paid well enough to afford them. But his taste is peerless; his business instincts unparalleled; his care for other people, for history and for the earth itself irrefutably compassionate. In 2021, after refusing to lay off workers or cut salaries during the Covid pandemic, he spoke alongside the then Prince Charles at the G20 summit to present his principles of humanistic capitalism and human sustainability. Guided by the philosophies of Pythagoras and Aristotle, he maintains a belief in work and life both championing the “moral and economic dignity of the human being.” That means turning “his company into a big family,” where the lights go out in his factory workrooms at the same time each day so everyone can eat homemade rigatoni together.
	

	It’s a sumptuously mounted effort, a romantic story of ambition and vision. Nicola Piovani’s score evokes a whimsical longing for every era of the designer’s life, as if the audience cheerfully lived it along with him. It’s possible, even likely, that he is as unambiguously wonderful in thought and deed as Tornatore and his army of co-conspirators claim. And in an era of unscrupulous capitalism, it’s a welcome fantasy to hear the story of a billionaire with compassion. But whether or not interview access was at all controlled by the film’s namesake production company, the experts and fans (among them Patrick Dempsey) are all sourced from a rarified social and financial strata that fails to even gesture towards a sense of completeness, much less objectivity.

	Concluding the film with an extremely long tracking shot of a table where Cucinelli sits at the head, Tornatore suggests that the designer accomplished his goal of turning his company into a family, everyone together enjoying the fruits of his success in an Italian landscape that defines “picturesque.” Like virtually every other goal outlined before that one, “Brunello: The Gracious Visionary” once again validates his worldview and supplies emotional gratification to the audience. (This kind of business practice is the way it should be, dammit!) But does it deliver truth? It feels like Tornatore has created the cinematic equivalent of one of Cucinelli’s garments: a film that’s covetable and frequently exquisite, but unless you belong to a certain echelon, its true value feels either unreal or completely unattainable.

schema.headline: ‘Brunello: The Gracious Visionary’ Review: Giuseppe Tornatore’s Seductive Hagiography of a Fashion Legend

title: ‘Hadestown: The Musical’ Review: Captures the Crowd-Pleasing Vibrance of the Mythological New Orleans-Meets-Rock Opera Stage Show
description: There’s a certain kind of Broadway musical that’s so fresh and brash and effusive it can seem as if the very form of the show is bursting right out
body:
There’s a certain kind of Broadway musical that’s so fresh and brash and effusive it can seem as if the very form of the show is bursting right out of its creators’ need to tell it. “A Chorus Line” was like that. So were “Chicago” and “Rent” and “Hamilton.” And while I won’t claim that “Hadestown” is the equal of those shows, it’s a musical that catches you up not merely in the story it’s telling but in the vivacious, spilling-over-the-sides structure of the show’s design.
	

	“Hadestown: The Musical,” a movie version that records and presents a live performance of the show that took place in February 2025 in London (much as the 2020 film of “Hamilton” presented a live production of that show), offers a splendid opportunity for anyone who hasn’t seen “Hadestown” onstage to experience it. The audience we see at this production at the West End’s Lyric Theatre is so in love with the show that you feel every person there has already seen it three times. And maybe that’s the case, since “Hadestown,” with its free-form jamboree vibe, its spontaneous swirl of musicians and dancers onstage, is as much a happening as it is a musical. It’s a show about ancient mythology — it tells the story of Orpheus and Eurydice, which it interweaves with the tale of Hades and Persephone. That sounds daunting, but “Hadestown,” with its book, music, and lyrics by Anaïs Mitchell, succeeds in making those myths feel timeless, which of course they are. It’s a show about love, but more than that it’s a show about faith.


	There is one set, and it looks like the grand interior of a moldering mansion in the late-afternoon sun if it were the New Orleans home of Dracula and he was a bootlegging gangster. The music, in a song like “Way Down Hadestown,” has a jaunty New Orleans spirit (especially when the trombone gets going), but much of the score is more eclectic than that — it’s a collage of brass-band exuberance and rock-musical passion and gospel ecstasy. One number, “Wedding Song,” sounds like “Can’t Find My Way Home” from the Blind Faith album. The lyrics to one of the best songs, “When the Chips Are Down,” play like an update of Madonna’s “Material World.” The show uses its infectious array of musical styles to evoke a big tent of rootsy Americana, and since most of the action is sung, it all has the feel of a patchwork opera.  
	

	The figure who draws us into “Hadestown” is Hermes, the herald of the gods who’s also the show’s narrator. He’s played by the Broadway legend André De Shields, who is now 80, and in a crisp silver three-piece suit, his whitish hair beaming off his head like an aureole, De Shields, with his diffident impish manner, his wavery slow vibrato, and his sunken cheeks that bespeak a pain he will not share, creates a presence of mystical authority. He’s down-home but larger-than-life, and so is the entire show.

	In mixing the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice with the romantic travails of Hades, the king of the underworld, “Hadestown” creates a romantic saga with a distinct echo of the one in “Moulin Rouge!” In that classic 2001 movie (as well as the Broadway version that premiered in 2018), Christian and Satine were bohemian lovers, while the Duke of Monroth was the moneybags conniver who thought he could buy Satine’s love. In “Hadestown,” Orpheus (Reeve Carney), a struggling poet and songwriter, meets the impoverished Eurydice (Eva Noblezada), and the two fall in love. But they can barely subsist. Hades (Patrick Page), portrayed as a demonic executive who presides over an underworld foundry, has driven away his wife, Persephone (Amber Gray), and he persuades Eurydice to come down to Hadestown, where he will love and protect her. She’s desperate enough to make a deal with the devil.

	If and when somebody pulls it together to make the Jeff Buckley biopic, I think we now have the actor to play him. It is Reeve Carney. He looks like Buckley, and has his floppy-haired louche glamour, but more than that he sings like him, with a keening high tenor that’s spellbinding. He makes Orpheus a character who’s a pure expressive force, a vessel of love and art and the vulnerability that comes of valuing both. Eva Noblezada, as Eurydice (she and Carney met during the early stage production of “Hadestown” and are now married), has a voice of ardent richness and a presence of traumatized devotion. And Patrick Page as Hades, the capitalist oppressor in his long leather coat, presiding over his factory world, lends the drama the villainous force it needs, although his Hades is far from inhuman. Page, tall and sculpted, with elegant white hair and a matching beard, is like Ian McKellan crossed with Christopher Lee. When Orpheus travels to Hadestown to retrieve Eurydice, and Hades agrees to let her go (under the condition that Orpheus can never once look back at her during the long journey home), he has designed this infamous conundrum as an elevated test. It will be the test of Orpheus’s faith, and watching the journey we in the audience contemplate what any of us might do. What does it mean…to look back?
	

	The show feels like a street dance crossed with a concert (at one point the musicians are introduced by name) that happens to have a hallowed myth threaded down the middle of it. The three Fates (Bella Brown, Madeline Charlemagne, and Allie Daniel) orbit the action like spitfire satellites. As directed by Brett Sullivan, “Hadestown: The Musical” transmits the show’s earthy electricity. That said, it’s still striking that the bare-bones film version of a Broadway musical that isn’t “Hamilton” is going to make $10 million at the box office this weekend. As the audience response to it in the movie makes clear, “Hadestown” is a show with a worshipful following. The movie made me a believer.

schema.headline: ‘Hadestown: The Musical’ Review: Captures the Crowd-Pleasing Vibrance of the Mythological New Orleans-Meets-Rock Opera Stage Show

title: Roxette Cancels 40th Anniversary Tour of North American Amphitheaters, Citing ‘Hugely Increased Touring Costs’
description: There was good news and bad news about Roxette‘s enduring popularity this week. The good news was, the group’s 1990 smash “It Must Have Been Love” w
body:
There was good news and bad news about Roxette‘s enduring popularity this week. The good news was, the group’s 1990 smash “It Must Have Been Love” was announced as having officially joined YouTube’s Billion Views Club. The bad news is, the audience that wants to hear that track performed live may not have been as great as anticipated, at least in North America.

	Roxette’s 40th anniversary tour had all of its U.S. and Canada dates canceled on Friday, with ticketholders receiving notices that their money was being refunded for the shows — despite the group itself issuing a statement that the tour was merely being “postponed.” The shows had been booked into amphitheaters in North America, with the Swedish act headlining a triple bill that also included fellow ’80s favorites Taylor Dayne and Nick Lowe.
	

	A statement on Roxette’s social media read: “Due to logistics and hugely increased touring costs, Live Nation US has decided to postpone the Northamerican (sic) tour. Hope to see you some other time down the road.” The announcement was signed “Team Rox.”


	Later on Saturday, founder founder/co-frontman Per Gessle added a personal note, telling fans the decision was strictly Live Nation’s. “Lena (Philipsson, the new singer), I and the band are of course disappointed. We were really looking forward to this northamerican tour and US is by far our biggest streaming market. This decision was made by Live Nation USA, which they probably based on their own calculations. I hope we can play for our fab fans in the USA and Canada at some point in the near future.” (Variety has reached out to Live Nation for comment.)
	


	The North American tour was to have begun Sept. 10 at Pine Knob Music Theatre in Clarkston, Michigan, and was scheduled to hit the Greek Theatre in Los Angeles on Oct. 5 before concluding Oct. 9 at White River Amphitheatre in Washington.

	Some fans expressed disappointment in the cancellation after having paid for nonrefundable flights to come into the U.S. from overseas to see the shows. But the number of foreign tourists who’d planned to see concerts in North America may speak to the common belief that Roxette had always been bigger in Europe than the U.S.

	Social media also brought up instances of fans saying they did not plan to buy tickets for the tour because the group was not the same without its late lead singer. Marie Fredriksson died in 2019 of complications from a brain tumor first diagnosed in the early 2000s. The band last did a limited series of dates with Fredriksson in 2016.



	

	



	In 2025, Gessle revived the group with a new female lead singer taking Fredriksson’s place, Swedish star Lena Philipsson. “I co-wrote Lena’s first major hit back in 1986 and she’s one of the brightest shining stars Sweden has ever known,” Gessle said in a statement at the time. “I’m extremely proud she wants to join me in my trek to keep the Roxette legacy alive.”

	The new Roxette continues to tour successfully overseas. This past week, they did shows in the Czech Republic and Austria. Between now and the end of August, they have shows still on the books for Germany, Denmark, Finland and Switzerland. 

	In a press release when the tour was announced, Live Nation called out Roxette’s enviable track record of hits. “With more than 80 million albums sold and a countless number of No. 1 hits across Europe, the U.S., Latin America and Asia, Roxette remains the Swedish act with the most U.S. Billboard No. 1 singles, four in total,” the promoter said.
	

	Roxette’s exit from the North American tour circuit follows a highly publicized wave of cancellations and postponements that have come to be popularly known as “blue dot fever,” referring to the sea of unsold tickets visible on seating charts for weak-selling concerts. The “fever” part of the saying was coined around the time that Zayn Malik cited unspecified health issues as the reason for calling off his U.S. tour.

	Other artists who’ve canceled either entire tours or significant chunks of their dates this year range from the Pussycat Dolls to Meghan Trainor to the only partially nixed Post Malone/Jelly Roll stadium tour. This month, Lily Allen canceled almost all of her dates in U.S. arenas and booked new shows in more modest amphitheaters. David Lee Roth joined the list of acts calling off the remainder of their dates this week. Kiefer Sutherland was among the few candid enough to outrightly acknowledge “poor ticket sales” for a tour cancellation. Of course, weak sales are not the only reason for taking a show off the road. Some artists have nixed dates due to what are considered to be legitimate health reasons, including such reliable ticket-sellers as Dolly Parton, the Beach Boys and Barry Manilow.

	Despite the wave of news media reports about cancellations in 2026, the overall touring business continues to be robust. Some industry observers, though, have sounded an alarm that increasingly high prices for superstar tours which are guaranteed instant sellouts may be siphoning off consumer dollars from mid-level acts, whose ticket prices are also going up. While Roxette’s cited “hugely increased touring costs” may not be the only reason for canceling a tour, the uptick in expenses that can turn a break-even tour into a money-loser is not a fallacy.

schema.headline: Roxette Cancels 40th Anniversary Tour of North American Amphitheaters, Citing ‘Hugely Increased Touring Costs’

title: Andy Roddick Lands First Major Acting Role in ‘The Dink’: ‘He’s Always Funny, but He’s on Another Level in This Movie,’ Says Star Jake Johnson
description:
Andy Roddick makes his acting debut playing a version of himself in the new pickleball sports comedy “The Dink.”

	The film’s star Jake Johnson and
body:
Andy Roddick makes his acting debut playing a version of himself in the new pickleball sports comedy “The Dink.”

	The film’s star Jake Johnson and the tennis champion had appeared on each other’s podcasts prior to making the movie.

	“He’s always funny, but he’s on another level in this movie,” Johnson told me at “The Dink” premiere on Monday. “We almost cast like a comedic actor to pretend to be an athlete, and we gambled and cast Andy and he crushes it.”
	

	It was producer Ben Stiller’s idea to offer the role to Roddick.


	“[Roddick’s] whole thing is he was very self-deprecating and he’s like, ‘I promise you I’m not the guy,’” Johnson said. “We were like, ‘You’re the guy. You’re the guy.’”

	He certainly was. “I think if you can compete at the level he competed in with sports, you can deal with a little bit of pressure and say some lines,” Johnson said. “He was open. He was funny. He was collaborative.”

	Johnson leads “The Dink” as a former tennis pro trying to gain his father’s respect by joining a pickleball club. The film, directed by Josh Greenbaum, also features Ed Harris, Chloe Fineman, Mary Steenburgen, Aaron Chen and Clio King.

	Greenbaum said of Roddick, “I had a Zoom with him and I was like, I think this guy can pull the role off…Any actor will tell you even if you’re playing a version of yourself, you still gotta act and he did an amazing job.”

	“The Dink” is available to stream on Apple TV.

schema.headline: Andy Roddick Lands First Major Acting Role in ‘The Dink’: ‘He’s Always Funny, but He’s on Another Level in This Movie,’ Says Star Jake Johnson

title: ‘Bob’s Burgers’ to Unveil New Holiday Short ‘On the Fort Day of Christmas’ This Year on Hulu

body:
‘Tis the season for “Bob’s Burgers,” which will return to the holidays with an all-new Christmas-themed short set to premiere on Hulu (and internationally for most Disney+ subscribers) later this year.

	Here’s the description for the short, titled “On the Fort Day of Christmas”: “a record-breaking Christmas snowstorm means one thing to the Belcher kids — a record-breaking Christmas snow fort.”


	At the “Bob’s Burgers” San Diego Comic-Con panel today, July 25 in Ballroom 20, 
	

	“Bob’s Burgers” creator and executive producer Loren Bouchard announced “On the Fort Day of Christmas” at San Diego Comic-Con on Saturday during their panel. Also on the panel with were H. Jon Benjamin (Bob Belcher), John Roberts (Linda Belcher), Kristen Schaal (Louise Belcher), Eugene Mirman (Gene Belcher), Dan Mintz (Tina Belcher) and supervising director Bernard Derriman.

	“On the Fort Day of Christmas” reps the first exclusive short from “Bob’s Burgers” to be produced for Hulu. The series previously released the show “My Butt Has a Fever,” which premiered in theaters and later FXX in 2022. Other extensions of the hit series include “The Bob’s Burgers Movie,” which was also released in 2022.

	“Bob’s Burgers” is back for Season 17 on Fox in midseason (early 2027), and streams the next day on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+ (for bundle subscribers in the U.S.).

	20th Television Animation is behind “Bob’s Burgers,” which was created and is executive produced by Loren Bouchard. Nora Smith, Dan Fybel, Rich Rinaldi, Jon Schroeder, Steven Davis, Scott Jacobson, Holly Schlesinger, Wendy Molyneux, Lizzie Molyneux-Logelin and Janelle Momary-Neely are also executive producers. The series was co-developed by Jim Dauterive.

body:
SPOILER ALERT: This article contains spoilers for “Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender.” 

	Team Avatar is back! 

	At long last, fans of “Avatar: The Last Airbender” can (legally) watch the next onscreen adventure of Aang and his loyal friends, thanks to the release of “Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender” on Paramount+.


	The film ages up Aang, Katara, Sokka, Toph and Zuko. Aang is well-established as the Avatar, but he is haunted by the fact that he is still the last airbender in the world.
	

	After a battle with a group of anti-benders calling themselves The Denied, Aang learns of the existence of a “lost Avatar,” an airbender named Sonam, who possessed a staff of immeasurable power. In his search for the staff, Aang discovers an ancient airbender named Tagah (voiced by Dave Bautista) frozen on top of a mountain. 

	Upon awakening Tagah, he tells the group that Sonam granted him and others the ability to become airbenders with her staff thousands of years ago. Figuring The Denied plan to use the staff to upset the fragile peace that now exists in the world, Team Avatar and Tagah set out to stop them. But along the way, they learn that Tagah witnessed the massacre of the other airbenders at the hands of the Earth Kingdom. He tried to overthrow Sonam and to use the staff to get revenge, leading to his imprisonment and Sonam exiling herself. 

	Aang and his friends must now battle Tagah and The Denied to once again save the world. 

	Variety spoke with “Avatar” creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko and the film’s director, Lauren Montgomery, about the launch of the movie, bringing “Avatar” back to the screen, and what ideas and characters didn’t make it into the final cut. 
	

	Check out the full Q&A below.  
	
		Why was this movie and story the point at which you wanted to re-enter the world of “Avatar?”	

	Michael Dante DiMartino: Obviously, Bryan and I came back to Nickelodeon to start Avatar Studios and start developing new projects to expand “Avatar” in TV and film. But film was the first priority for the studio, so we set to work thinking about what that would look like. There wasn’t too much debate that we would focus on the original characters since they were the most iconic and most beloved characters we had so far. Then we quickly sort of settled on — for this to feel bigger and different, and an extension of the story we had already told, that aging them up, meeting them at a later point in their life, seemed like a good way to drop into the world again.

	Bryan Konietzko: I might be an outlier, but — I still wanted to work in the “Avatar” world, but I wasn’t hungry to go back to the original characters because that was the story that Mike and I set out to tell, and we were lucky enough to be able to complete it. And I wanted those characters to kind of have some peace and privacy and go on with their lives, and explore other parts of the Avatar world. But yeah, the studio and Mike said, if we’re going to do a big feature film, it does make sense to focus on the main characters. But it wasn’t until Mike pitched to me the idea of them at this age that the door sort of opened for me creatively.

	We had originally thought of it being when Aang and Katara were about to start their family, and for a lot of good reasons, we moved away from that later in development. But I still found this moment in Aang’s life to be really interesting. It’s like, you look like an adult, you have adult responsibilities, but you haven’t quite shed your adolescence. He’s also the age that I was when Mike and I created “Avatar.” I was 25 going on 26, and so I had a lot of youthful enthusiasm, but I had a lot to learn about the world…We had this cool poster that Joaquim Dos Santos had drawn during “Korra” of the original Team Avatar all around that age, and I think all of us and a lot of fans just kind of wondered, like, “Wow, what would that be like?”

	Lauren Montgomery: These are the characters that you fell in love with…How are you going to tell another really satisfying story about [Aang]? And I think like the beauty of what we found is the only really personal story left to tell about Aang, and just the fact that it was always in the title, was being the last Airbender. We’ve seen his arc of becoming the Avatar, but now we handle that other side. There was something really beautiful and emotional still to tell in that story. I was excited just because I very much love a tortured, emotional story. Even though I dislike drama in my life, I love it in my content.
	
	
		Like the shows, there are some crazy big action sequences in this. What was different about making them for a movie versus a series? 	

	Montgomery: The craziest thing was we were making it, and I’m looking at this movie, and I’m like, “There’s not enough action!” There’s just so much action, but there’s so many things, so many ideas, like for Tagah. We had so many awesome conversations about his fighting style, and we didn’t even get to get all of it in there. There were so many things we discussed, and I wish we could have fit it, but ultimately, there was a lot of story to be told.

	It was really exciting to be able to work with Alfred Hsing. Bryan and Mike had met him at Netflix. He’s an amazing choreographer, and we worked together just discussing concepts of how the characters would have evolved in their fighting styles and discovering Tagah’s style and what that means as an airbender, but as an airbender that uses his air bending in different ways. There was a lot in this movie as far as using bending to fight like other martial artist opponents and also using bending to fight natural disasters. So we tackled everything, and yet I still feel like there’s so much we didn’t get to do.

	Konietzko: We had the benefit of doing [previsualization] this time, which we kind of dabbled in “Korra” with just one compositor, but Lauren and the team were able to — like you said, these set pieces, they involved such a much more cinematic and kind of active camera. One that could flow through a three-dimensional space, but with two-dimensional, hand-drawn characters, and that process always takes a lot of pre-planning.

	DiMartino: When we were doing the series, our ambition in our brains was always thinking cinematically, but we were limited by time and money and the old aspect ratio of television back in the day. But when we made the finale of “Avatar,” we did screen it as — and we have screened it since then — the four parts as one movie, and it does hold up. You know, it feels like a big experience, a movie experience, even though the visuals aren’t quite at the level that this movie is at.
	
		This also has a pretty different art style than both “Last Airbender” and “Legend of Korra.” Why did you go that route? 	

	Konietzko: We always want each “Avatar” project to have its own distinct visual identity. At the same time, we want them all to feel like they hang with each other. That way they’re different windows into the same world. And a common factor or characteristic of that is that each one is a love letter to Japanese anime…
	

	I learned a lot in in making the first series, but we also had some incredible talent that rose to the surface between “Avatar” and “Korra.” And one of those folks was Ki Hyun Ryu. He did some amazing stuff on “Avatar,” and then he ended up being a supervisor, alongside Lauren, on “Korra,” and so even on Korra, we started basing the character design largely inspired by Ryu’s style.

	DiMartino: There is an incredible amount of handcrafted attention to this movie, even though obviously computers are used for all the camera moves, and everyone’s drawing on tablets or whatever, but these look like oil paintings come to life. Every frame, somebody drew that multiple times. They roughed it out, and someone had to clean it up, and someone had to paint every frame. And then there’s the whole compositing aspect to it too, which is another process. Every frame is being gone over very carefully to make sure it all works and feels cohesive.

	Montgomery: There’s a lot of technology used, but those are just the tools. Human artists crafted everything, and human artists used that technology to direct those shots. Nothing was just like plug it in and boop boop, it happens. There’s none of that
	
		This project and what I’ve seen of “Seven Havens” have distinctly Indian influences. From Avatar Sonam being voiced by Freida Pinto to even the music. There’s one singer in particular — 	

	Konietzko: Varijashree Venugopal! Jeremy [Zuckerman], our composer, he was connected with her by a friend. We’re working with Jeremy and Varijashree together on another one of our projects. And I’m just like, “You two are a match made in the spirit world.”

	With “Seven Havens,” it was very deliberate. The concept and even the word “avatar” all comes from Indian culture and tradition and Sanskrit. So we had done a bit in “Avatar,” the original series. We’re obviously inspired by and draw from a lot of real world cultures for our fantasy world. But that said, I kind of felt like with the first two series, we had underserved that inspiration, and so it was very deliberate with Seven Havens to to code Pavi as a South Asian-inspired character.

	Montgomery: We definitely wanted to lean into those ancient cultures’ mysticism, more fantasy, more spirituality, and I think a lot of that is apparent in a lot of the Indian cultures. Then we were just trying to really add to that ethereal quality of [Avatar Sonam], and Varijashree’s voice just gives you that. It’s so haunting.
	
	
		Talk to me about the challenges of trying to make a story that follows “Last Airbender” but also stays consistent with the story you established later in the timeline with “Legend of Korra.” How challenging is that? 	

	Konietzko: Oh, it’s a nightmare [laughs]. It’s really hard.

	DiMartino: I do like that part of the job where it’s just like figuring out the puzzle pieces. It gets more complex, obviously, with every year and every project we’re adding to this stuff. But yeah, part of what I do now is — whether it’s publishing or games or whatever — it’s like, does this feel like it actually fits in the overall universe? It’s not completely contradicting something else in another project. There are little tweaks we make, but if someone in a comic said this line, and it doesn’t match with this, we might be like, “That’s not the end of the world.” Because there’s so many different writers at this point who contribute ideas and stuff. So it’s hard to police every line of dialog or every line in a novel or something.

	Obviously, we couldn’t end the movie where the airbenders are back. That obviously would not work. So there’s those kind guardrails on it where it’s like, okay, we know that’s not the end of the movie. So what is a satisfying end to this where Aang still feels like he achieved something and is in a better place?
	
		And Tagah is obviously very central to the film. Talk to me about establishing him as this very dark airbender, and also what it was like getting to work with Dave Bautista as the voice of the character. 	

	DiMartino: That character, like with a lot of things in the movie, went through a big evolution. There was a point where he wasn’t in the movie, and then there was a version of Tagah that came into the movie, but he was named something else. But then once we settled that Aang finds another airbender, that’s the crux of this film, this brotherhood, this bond they form, and their different points of view. Since he’s from this time long ago, they would have these interpersonal conflicts. But also there’s the idea that they kind of mirror of each other. They’ve both gone through this genocide of their people, just at different times in the history of universe. Then we see how they both deal with that conflict in different ways and how that brings them closer and pulls them apart.
	

	Montgomery: I didn’t follow wrestling. I didn’t know Dave. I just knew him from his movie roles. But either way, Drax and his wrestling persona are big personas, and I think I was expecting him to be a very big persona guy, and he’s actually like the gentlest, kindest human I have met. He doesn’t speak very loudly, he’s very respectful, and he really feels like the good version of Tagah that we see. He’s like this monk who is saving a bird in the middle of the ocean. So it was really incredible that it kind of wound up that way, because like Mike said, there was a different character originally that was just a very different personality. And when we found this character of Tagah, who just brought so much more to the story, it’s kind of amazing how beautifully Dave was able to make that character feel like he has so much more of a history and a depth.
	
		Can you tell me any ideas you had that didn’t make it into the movie? 	

	DiMartino: I know fans are going to be upset. Suki’s not in the movie. She’s in one shot at the end. We did try versions where Suki was in the movie. You just have to make these decisions where it’s like, we only have 85 minutes to tell the story. We were already having a hard time giving our beloved main characters their spotlight and enough screen time… The Kyoshi Warriors are out there! They were off saving somebody else while the events of this movie were going on. Doesn’t mean they’re not around. They have their own comic book series now, so they are busy ladies.

	Montgomery: There was a scene that I really loved that didn’t quite make it into the final film, and it was this parade that was the celebration of Republic City… It was so beautiful, and you saw a lot of fun Easter eggs of people. I think King Kuei was there, Suki was there with the Kyoshi Warriors, and it was this magnificent celebration of everyone celebrating their cultures…and then the final person in this parade is Aang on Appa, and it becomes a perspective shift where you realize what is so joyous for everyone is very isolating for Aang, and he never feels more alone than in this moment, where everyone else can celebrate with their culture, and his is absent.
	
		Finally, the movie is getting a limited awards qualifying run in theaters instead of a full theatrical release. But the tickets for the awards screenings sold out in a day, I think. 	

	DiMartino: I think it sold out in like 10 minutes or something.
	

	Konietzko: Yeah, it was pretty quick.

	DiMartino: I think that just shows that people really want to see this movie.

	Konietzko: I’m still trying to get tickets to a Paramount screening! I got locked out of that. I’m texting my executive like, “Hey, can I maybe get a couple tickets?” [laughs]

	This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

title: President Trump Experiences Awkward Jeffrey Epstein Moment During White House Correspondents' Dinner
description:
White House Correspondents' Dinner
                          Trump Smiles, Shrugs During Awkward
body:
White House Correspondents' Dinner
                          Trump Smiles, Shrugs During Awkward Epstein Moment
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 25, 2026
                            5:07 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            President Donald Trump couldn't duck these two words -- Jeffrey Epstein -- at Friday night's White House Correspondents' Dinner -- and it made for a seriously awkward moment.
      
    
            The moment came when CNN anchor Wolf Blitzer announced that The Wall Street Journal had won the 2026 Katharine Graham Award for Courage and Accountability for the newspaper's big scoop on Trump's past relationship with Epstein -- the late convicted pedophile financier.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Twitter Tweet.
      
    
            Trump just smiled and shrugged his shoulders after Blitzer told the crowd the prez had filed a $20 billion lawsuit against The Journal, which included the home address of Khadeeja Safdar -- one of the reporters on the groundbreaking story.
      

            Blitzer also said Safdar's family was forced to relocate as a result of their address going public ... but Trump just brushed it off with a smile. Then, after Safdar accepted her award from Blitzer, Trump stood up and shook her hand, and some would call their interaction awkward -- just see it for yourself above.
      
    
            Standing at a podium, Blitzer introduced WSJ's investigation into Epstein and his relationship with Trump, as Trump looked on from his seat nearby in the packed ballroom of D.C.'s Waldorf Astoria hotel. Blitzer said the WSJ's reporting triggered the release of the Epstein files, thousands of pages of documents that might have otherwise been concealed from the public.
      
    
            As you know, Trump previously declared the Epstein Files are a hoax.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Wolf also said the Journal courageously published its story -- despite Trump's threat of a lawsuit -- along with a provocative letter to Epstein allegedly bearing Trump's signature.
      
    
            As WSJ reported, Epstein was given a photo album for his 50th birthday that contained the letter with a drawing of a naked woman and Trump's purported signature ... you can see it above.
      
    
            Trump just can't shake Epstein.

title: Nolan Wells' Best Friend Explains Why He Skipped Funeral
description:
Nolan Wells' Best Friend
                          Death Threats Scared Me Away From Funeral
body:
Nolan Wells' Best Friend
                          Death Threats Scared Me Away From Funeral
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              July 25, 2026
                            1:03 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Nolan Wells' best friend says he skipped his pal's funeral for multiple reasons ... including multiple threats he says he's received in recent days.
      
    
            Warren Hudson opened up about the difficult decision to stay away from Nolan's service during an interview on "The Officer Tatum Show" ... revealing he chose to skip it first and foremost to not distract from the event's focus on Nolan and his grieving family.
      
    
            He then adds that he worried about going to such a public gathering, too ... saying he's received thousands of death threats -- and he didn't want to put himself or his family in danger.
      

            Warren says it's horrible he had to make that choice ... but it's just the reality of his life recently.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The interview with Brandon Tatum has been chock-full of stunning revelations ... with Warren insisting he had nothing to do with Nolan's death -- and even telling a story about how Nolan refused his group's pleas to leave the island with them.
      
    
            It's not unusual on Horn Island to arrive on one boat and leave on another, Warren told Brandon ... but the group didn't want Nolan to stay on the island -- which Warren also admits in the interview can be dangerous.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As you know ... Nolan went missing on Fourth of July weekend earlier this month -- and his body was later found off the coast of Horn Island in the Mississippi Gulf Coast.
      
    
            Authorities initially posited Nolan drowned ... but his parents and their attorney, Ben Crump, insist they don't buy the official narrative -- and even had their own autopsy performed.
